# Solution Concept & Originality

Advising on mobility subscriptions needs the recommendation to be numerically right and its reasoning understandable to someone who won't audit a spreadsheet. We split those demands across dedicated components: deterministic pricing and scoring engines, a single LangGraph agent backed by a university-hosted GPT endpoint for the conversation, a FastAPI/PostgreSQL service layer underneath, and Langfuse tracing every model call. Chapter 3 covers how these fit together; we avoided a fully agentic pipeline so a number's reliability never depends on how a conversation happens to go.

We are not aware of a consumer product that already does this: pull a customer's multi-provider travel history together, price it against the market, and execute the resulting change itself rather than leaving that to the customer. That gap is also why the idea is harder than it sounds: once a system can act on real contracts, a guessed number or an unsupervised execution stops being a wrong chat answer and becomes a costly mistake. The value on offer is exactly that: a portfolio review and, if wanted, the change carried out, without the customer doing either piece of work.

The brief's advanced tier suggested a four-agent split, i.e. one LLM agent each for analysis, forecasting, optimization and communication. That is the standard tutorial move of decomposing a workflow into tasks and giving each its own agent. We asked instead whether a language model was the right tool for each task at all. For pricing, eligibility and scoring the answer was no, so three of the four roles became deterministic engines, and only the fourth survived as an agent, alongside two narrowly scoped LLM steps inside the pipeline. That restraint also makes the system measurable: the deterministic engines' output serves as ground truth for the naive single-LLM-call baseline evaluated in Chapter 6, a comparison a four-agent design built entirely from language-model reasoning could not offer.
